scope: All 50 states, D.C. and five territories. State general fund and rainy-day balances (NASBO Spring 2026), state all-funds spending and its split by six functions (NASBO SER 2025, state government only), fiscal-year start and budget cycle (NASBO 2021), line-item veto and late-budget rules. Per-place Census combined state-and-local revenue and spending are supplied by state-local-finances-2022.json; this file records only the national snippet values under national.

rainyDayFund.note: Totals for FY2026 and FY2027 carry forward the last reported balance for states that could not report (Georgia, Wisconsin; plus Mississippi and Virginia for FY2027).

stateSpendingByFunctionFY2025Percent.basis: all states, state government only, all funds

fiscalYearPattern.rule: 46 states start July 1; Alabama and Michigan October 1; New York April 1; Texas September 1. Federal government and D.C. October 1. Puerto Rico July 1; Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands October 1.
fiscalYearPattern.evidence: states verified-in-document (2021); NCSL 2025 snippet agrees on the four exceptions; territories snippet-derived

lineItemVeto.note: NASBO's 43 also leaves out Maryland, where the governor cannot veto the operating budget bill at all but can item-veto supplementary and capital appropriations. The spec's 44 matches NCSL.

results.finding: AGREES. NASBO: the year may end in deficit, but the next budget must be balanced.

results.92N: no balanced-budget requirement at any stage
results.finding: AGREES. NASBO: Vermont is the one state with no legal requirement; a deficit has never been carried over in practice.
DISAGREES on stage 4. NASBO: Indiana may carry over annual deficits and has no requirement to fix them next cycle, though it cannot take on debt except narrowly.
DISAGREES on stage 4. NASBO: spending above revenue covered by the rainy-day fund is carried into the next year, which must cut to rebalance.
DISAGREES. NCSL (44 states) and NASBO Table 8 both give Maine a line-item veto of appropriation amounts, overridden by a majority of elected members. 92N counts 43 states; NCSL counts 44.

congressionalReview.rule: D.C.'s local budget is set out in the annual federal appropriations act and is subject to congressional review under the Home Rule Act. The 2012 Local Budget Autonomy Amendment Act (approved by 83 percent of D.C. voters) provides for a 30-day layover instead, but Congress continued to act on D.C.'s budget: the March 2025 full-year continuing resolution held D.C.'s own local funds to FY2024 levels (about a $1.1 billion cut) until a fix passed; a later FY2026 act's Division E formally approved the FY2026 local budget.

lateBudget.rule: Tied to federal appropriations; a federal shutdown or continuing resolution can restrict D.C. spending of local funds unless Congress provides otherwise.
